name: Probiotics
summary: Probiotics are live microorganisms supplied in foods or supplements for intended health benefits. Products can contain bacteria, yeasts, or mixtures; the exact strain matters, not just the word probiotic.
commonUses: Used in products marketed for digestive health
Used in products marketed for the gut microbiome
roles: Probiotic ingredients are living microorganisms, not vitamins or minerals.
Different microorganisms can interact with the gut and immune system in different ways; results for one strain do not establish what another strain does.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test. It does not define a probiotic deficiency.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: Some yogurts and other fermented foods contain live microorganisms
foodSources.note: A fermented food is not automatically equivalent to a supplement containing a named strain.

forms.name: Bacterial strains
forms.note: Labels may name Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium species and a strain identifier. A species name alone does not identify the strain tested in research.

forms.name: Yeast probiotics
forms.note: Saccharomyces boulardii is a yeast, not a bacterial probiotic; it is a different ingredient.

forms.name: Mixtures and synbiotics
forms.note: Mixtures contain several microorganisms. Synbiotics combine probiotics with prebiotics, ingredients used by microorganisms; these products are not equivalent to each single strain.

reference.noUpperLimit: This basic guide does not provide reference intakes or upper-limit values.

interactions.with: Severe illness or a weakened immune system
interactions.note: Live microorganisms can cause infection in higher-risk people. Discuss a specific product with the treating clinician rather than treating probiotics as harmless food ingredients.

cautions: Serious infections are a greater concern in people with severe illness or a weakened immune system, including seriously ill hospital patients.
Severe and fatal infections have occurred in premature infants given probiotics. Infant use belongs with the baby's medical team, not a general supplement routine.
Some products have contained microorganisms not listed on their labels; contamination can pose serious health risks.
Safety and effects depend on the strain and product. A finding for one probiotic does not establish the safety or usefulness of another.
